question: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
Which ancient wonder of the world was located in Giza, Egypt?
What is the longest river in the world?
Who developed the theory of general relativity?
What gas do plants absorb from the atmosphere during photosynthesis?
What was the name of the first web browser, which doubled as a page editor?
What was the only HTTP method supported by the original HTTP/0.9 protocol?
What 1993 browser is usually credited with driving the Web's first mass adoption, years after it was invented?
What computer brand ran the entire World Wide Web in its first months?
Who coined the term "hypertext," the concept the Web was built on, decades before it existed?
About how many years did Michelangelo spend painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling?
Contrary to popular belief, Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in what position rather than lying on his back?
What art form did Michelangelo consider his true calling, having resented being pulled off a tomb commission to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling instead?
How many scenes from the Book of Genesis run along the center of the Sistine Chapel ceiling?
About how many individual figures did Michelangelo ultimately paint across the Sistine Chapel ceiling, far beyond the dozen apostles he was originally asked for?
What ordinary object does the Icelandic word "loki" literally mean — a clue that may finally explain the origin of the trickster god's name?
Despite his central role in the myths, what did Loki apparently never receive from real worshippers in pre-Christian Scandinavia, unlike Odin or Thor?
What common modern title for Loki — "god of ___" — never actually appears in the medieval texts that record his myths?
What 12th-century Danish chronicler wrote an extensive account of Norse mythology yet never once mentioned Loki?
In what country was the Snaptun Stone found, a carved hearthstone from around 1000 CE thought to show Loki with his lips scarred shut?
How many languages of spoken greetings does the Golden Record aboard Voyager 1 carry into interstellar space?
About how many watts of electrical output do Voyager 1's plutonium-powered generators lose every year as their fuel decays?
What science instrument did NASA permanently power down on Voyager 1 in April 2026 after a February roll maneuver nearly tripped its undervoltage safety fault?
As of 2026, about how many hours does a one-way radio signal take to cross the roughly 15 billion miles between Earth and Voyager 1?
About how many kilobytes of memory does Voyager 1's entire onboard computer system have — less than a single photo on a modern phone?
What molecule can a California two-spot octopus edit at over 13,000 sites within hours of a sudden cold shock, retuning its nervous system without changing a single letter of DNA?
About what fraction of an octopus's roughly 500 million neurons sit in its eight arms rather than its central brain?
Which of an octopus's three hearts stops beating every time it swims, making crawling along the seafloor the less exhausting way to get around?
What copper-based protein turns octopus blood blue and helps it carry oxygen efficiently in cold, low-oxygen water?
What discarded item does the veined octopus collect and haul across the seafloor to assemble into portable shelter later?
What microbial process, not roasting, is primarily responsible for turning bitter, astringent raw cacao beans into the precursors of chocolate flavor?
What dough, made from a common Aztec grain, did counterfeiters pack into hollowed-out cacao shells to pass fakes off as real currency beans?
What Dutch chemist's 1828 invention — pressing cacao butter out of ground cacao and alkalizing what remained — created modern cocoa powder and gave 'Dutch process' chocolate its name?
What bitter alkaloid in chocolate is harmless to humans but toxic to dogs, who metabolize it far more slowly than we do?
What process — controlled heating and cooling — forces cocoa butter into its stable crystal structure, giving good chocolate its snap, gloss, and melt-in-your-mouth feel?
What antimatter particle do the most powerful lightning-linked gamma-ray bursts, called terrestrial gamma-ray flashes, fire out into space?
What high-energy particles raining down from deep space are now thought to help seed the runaway electron avalanches that trigger lightning inside storm clouds?
What term describes the reddish, jellyfish-shaped electrical flashes that shoot from thunderstorm tops up into the mesosphere, first caught on video by accident in 1989?
What nickname do volcanologists use for the lightning storms that erupt inside a volcano's own ash plume?
What glassy, root-shaped tube of fused silica does a lightning strike leave behind when it hits sand?
What earlier disaster, 17 years before Vesuvius erupted, had already devastated Pompeii and left much of the city still mid-repair when the eruption hit?
Though tradition dates Vesuvius's eruption to August 24, AD 79, autumn produce and warm clothing on victims have led many scholars to now place it in what later month?
What Italian archaeologist began pouring plaster into the body-shaped voids in Pompeii's hardened ash in 1863, casting victims in their final poses?
What term describes the clenched, boxer-like pose baked into many Pompeii casts and skeletons, caused by heat-contracted muscles rather than a final struggle?
What organ was found vitrified, turned to glass, inside the skull of a young victim at Pompeii's sister city Herculaneum?
Who first spotted the mysterious repeated DNA sequences later named CRISPR, while studying E. coli in 1987, decades before anyone knew what they did?
What food company's research into yogurt- and cheese-fermenting bacteria first revealed that CRISPR works as a bacterial immune system against viruses?
About how many years passed between CRISPR's accidental discovery in bacterial DNA and scientists confirming it functions as an antiviral defense system?
Which gene does Casgevy, the first FDA-approved CRISPR-based therapy, edit in patients to treat sickle cell disease?
In 2020, Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna became the first all-female duo to share a Nobel Prize in what category, for their work on CRISPR-Cas9?
What geospatial engineer calculated the exact coordinates of Point Nemo in 1992 using computer software, without ever sailing there himself?
Because Point Nemo sits so far from any coastline, the crew of what orbiting outpost, passing about 400 km overhead, are often the closest humans to it?
What 120-ton Russian space station was deliberately deorbited and sunk into the Point Nemo spacecraft graveyard in 2001?
What massive rotating ocean current starves the waters around Point Nemo of nutrients, making it one of the most biologically lifeless patches of sea on Earth?
About how many decommissioned spacecraft have nations deliberately sunk at Point Nemo since 1971?
What 14th-century emperor of the Mali Empire is generally regarded as the wealthiest person in recorded history, thanks to his realm's near-monopoly on West African gold and salt trade routes?
Mansa Musa's lavish gold spending during a stopover devalued the currency of what city for over a decade afterward?
What Andalusian poet and architect did Mansa Musa recruit in Mecca to help design Timbuktu's Djinguereber Mosque?
What 1375 map by Majorcan cartographers first depicted Mansa Musa enthroned with a gold nugget, putting Mali on Europe's radar?
Roughly how many tons of gold did Mansa Musa reportedly carry with him on his hajj to Mecca?
What 2,000-year-old bronze device, recovered from a Greek shipwreck off Antikythera in 1901, is now recognized as the world's oldest known analog computer?
What ancient eclipse-prediction cycle of 223 lunar months was mechanically encoded in the Antikythera mechanism's spiral back dial?
What four-year Panhellenic athletic cycle, including the games at Olympia, did one of the Antikythera mechanism's small front dials track?
How many surviving bronze gears did modern X-ray and CT imaging reveal packed inside the corroded Antikythera mechanism?
Whose ancient theory of the Moon's uneven orbital speed did the Antikythera mechanism model more accurately than any written astronomy for centuries after, using a clever pin-and-slot gear?
What black-white-and-gray painting technique did Picasso use for Guernica to mimic the immediacy of wartime newsprint photography?
About how many weeks did Picasso take to paint the 25-foot-wide Guernica, working from May 1 to June 4, 1937?
What photographer, Picasso's partner at the time, documented Guernica's creation in a sequence of 28 studio photographs?
Guernica spent over 40 years on loan at what New York museum, per Picasso's decree that it not go to Spain until democracy was restored there?
Whose February 2003 speech to the UN Security Council advocating for the Iraq War prompted staff to cover the Guernica tapestry outside with a blue curtain?
What trickster spider-god from Akan folklore in Ghana is credited as the source of all stories, giving Ghanaian folktales their collective name?
According to Akan legend, which sky god sold Anansi the rights to all the world's stories, in exchange for him capturing a python, a leopard, a swarm of hornets, and a menacing forest spirit?
What Akan word, literally meaning something like "spider tales," became the general term Ghanaians use for any folktale, whether or not Anansi appears in it?
In one Anansi tale, to what part of his own body did he foolishly strap a pot containing all the world's wisdom before trying to climb a tree with it?
What name did enslaved Africans' descendants in the American South give to Anansi as his stories took root in Gullah and Southern oral tradition?
What kind of ultra-dense stellar remnant, left behind when a massive star's core collapses in a supernova, packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere about the size of a city?
About how many billion tons would a sugar-cube-sized piece of neutron-star material weigh if you could bring it to Earth?

What general class of super-fast-spinning neutron stars — which reach such speeds by siphoning matter and angular momentum from a companion star over millions of years — is exemplified by the record holder PSR J1748-2446ad, spinning about 716 times a second?

What type of neutron star, with a magnetic field trillions of times stronger than Earth's, unleashed a December 2004 flare so powerful it measurably disturbed Earth's ionosphere from 50,000 light-years away?
What runaway nuclear process, fueled by the neutron-rich debris of colliding neutron stars, is responsible for forging heavy elements like gold and platinum?
What oversized, jelly-like sugar polymer, secreted by naked mole-rat skin cells in a form over five times larger than the human version, is credited with making the species nearly immune to cancer?
About how many minutes can a naked mole-rat survive total oxygen deprivation by switching its brain's fuel from glucose to fructose?
What social structure, otherwise found almost only in insects like ants, bees, and termites, organizes naked mole-rat colonies around a single breeding queen?
What kind of sensation do naked mole-rats fail to feel, thanks to a mutated sodium channel, letting them shrug off the carbon dioxide buildup in their crowded, poorly ventilated tunnels?
About how many years, over ten times longer than a similarly sized mouse, can naked mole-rats live, making them the longest-lived rodent known?

What 19th-century technique for artificially pollinating vanilla orchids — still used on nearly every vanilla flower grown today — was invented in 1841 by a 12-year-old enslaved boy on the French island of Reunion?
Vanilla is often called the world's second-most-expensive spice by weight, trailing only which spice, hand-plucked three threads at a time from crocus flowers?
About what percentage of the world's vanilla supply comes from a single island nation, whose cyclones and droughts can send global prices swinging wildly?
What tough structural byproduct of pulping wood for paper served for much of the 20th century as the main raw material for cheap synthetic vanillin?
What do some Madagascar farmers prick into their still-green vanilla pods with a needle, as a kind of brand-like signature to deter theft during harvest season?

What narrow, sky-borne filament of concentrated water vapor carries most of the moisture reaching the world's mid-latitudes, flowing thousands of miles across an ocean before wringing out as rain or snow where it hits land?

Two researchers coined the term "atmospheric river" in the early 1990s, choosing wording that stressed how slender these moisture corridors are relative to their length. At what university did they work?
An average atmospheric river transports roughly 7 to 15 times as much water as pours from the mouth of which North American river, the largest by discharge in the United States?

One winter in the early 1860s, a weeks-long parade of atmospheric rivers turned California's Central Valley into an inland sea up to 300 miles long, bankrupting the young state and driving its legislature out of a flooded Sacramento; the USGS later modeled its 'ARkStorm' megaflood scenario on it. In what year did that flooding peak?

The intensity scale for atmospheric rivers unveiled in 2019 borrows the hurricane scale's 1-to-5 categories but adds a variable hurricanes ignore: a strong storm is bumped up a category when it stalls over one area past 48 hours. What is that added variable?
What Swedish warship, built as King Gustav II Adolf's flagship during the Thirty Years' War, capsized in Stockholm harbor barely a kilometer into its maiden voyage in 1628?
About how many minutes after setting sail did a gust of wind heel the Vasa far enough over for water to pour through its open gun ports and send it to the bottom?
What Swedish engineer spent years combing naval archives and dragging a homemade grapple through Stockholm harbor before locating the wreck of the Vasa in 1956?
What wood-boring mollusk, common in full-strength seawater but unable to tolerate the Baltic's low salt content, is the main reason the Vasa's hull survived on the seabed for over three centuries?

What corrosive substance is now slowly forming inside the raised Vasa's timbers, as sulfur compounds absorbed from centuries in the anoxic mud oxidize with the help of iron leaching from its corroding bolts?

What single term, coined in 1982 for an infectious agent made purely of misfolded protein with no DNA or RNA of its own, describes a particle that forces normal copies of that same protein to misfold in turn?

What caustic chemical, alongside prolonged high-temperature autoclaving well beyond routine hospital settings, is one of the few treatments known to reliably destroy prions clinging to surgical instruments?

What American virologist won the 1976 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for proving that kuru was a slow, transmissible infection, two decades before the 'prion' concept explained what was actually spreading it?
What Papua New Guinea highlands people experienced a devastating 20th-century kuru epidemic, tied to a mortuary rite in which relatives ate the tissue of their deceased kin?
What nickname, evoking a horror-movie label, has become the popular name for chronic wasting disease as it spreads through deer, elk, and moose herds across North America?
What arid depression in northeastern Ethiopia, sitting more than 100 meters below sea level at the meeting point of three tectonic plates, is regularly cited as the hottest inhabited place on Earth?

What geological term describes the point beneath the Danakil Depression where the Nubian, Somali, and Arabian tectonic plates are pulling apart, in a process expected to eventually flood the rift and form a new ocean?

What geothermal field in the Danakil Depression, with pools so acidic they sit near pH 0 and vivid yellow-green mineral crusts, draws scientists searching for microbial life that could hint at how organisms might survive on Mars?
What shield volcano in the Danakil Depression, whose Afar-language name translates to 'smoking mountain,' holds one of the world's few permanent lava lakes?
What name was given to the standardized bars of salt, cut from the Danakil Depression's flats and carried out by camel caravan, that once circulated as a form of currency across highland Ethiopia?

What Hungarian physician, working in a Vienna maternity ward in the 1840s, discovered that a simple hand-hygiene practice could slash deaths from childbed fever decades before germ theory was accepted?
What colleague's death from a scalpel wound picked up during an autopsy gave Semmelweis the key insight linking invisible 'cadaverous particles' to the deaths of new mothers on his ward?
What chemical solution did Semmelweis order doctors to scrub their hands in before examining maternity patients, a change that cut his ward's death rate from over 18% to around 1%?

What term, now used across science and medicine generally, describes the reflexive rejection of new evidence that contradicts accepted belief — the very reaction Semmelweis's hand-hygiene findings met from his own colleagues?

What blood infection, the same broad category of illness Semmelweis had devoted his career to preventing, ultimately killed him two weeks after he was committed to an asylum and allegedly beaten by guards?

What early 19th-century French weaving machine, controlled by a chain of interchangeable punched cards that dictated each row of its pattern, is now regarded as one of the first programmable machines in history?
What earlier French inventor, working decades before the Jacquard loom's creation, first used a punched paper roll to automate a loom's weaving pattern, laying the groundwork it was built on?
In what French silk-weaving city did workers, fearing the new Jacquard loom would destroy their livelihoods, reportedly smash the looms and burn Jacquard's effigy in the early 1800s?
About how many punched cards, each capable of over 1,000 hole positions, were reportedly needed to weave one particularly detailed silk portrait using the Jacquard loom's card-controlled technique?
What British mathematician, writing in 1843 about Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, compared its algebraic calculations to the way the Jacquard loom "weaves flowers and leaves"?

What Nantucket whaling ship, rammed and sunk by an enraged sperm whale in 1820 and leaving its crew adrift for months in an ordeal that included cannibalism, directly inspired the climax of Moby-Dick?

What real albino sperm whale, notorious among 19th-century Pacific whalers and profiled in an 1839 magazine article near a Chilean island, is thought to have lent Melville the idea of a giant white whale?

What crucial closing section of Moby-Dick did Melville's British publisher, releasing the book as 'The Whale,' accidentally omit — leaving British reviewers baffled about how a narrator who seemingly died with the ship could have told the story?
What name is given to the surge of critical and popular interest in Melville's work during the 1920s, decades after his 1891 death, that rescued Moby-Dick from near-obscurity?
About how many copies made up the first American printing of Moby-Dick in 1851 — a run so small that copies still hadn't sold out by the time Melville died four decades later?
What Nile fish, according to Egyptian myth, ate the one part of Osiris's body Isis could never recover — and lent its name to a major Egyptian city where it was later venerated?
Despite ruling over the dead, what color was Osiris's skin most often painted in Egyptian art — a hue tied to fertile Nile silt and sprouting crops rather than to decay?
What ancient pillar-shaped symbol, said to represent Osiris's restored backbone, was ceremonially "raised" during royal jubilee festivals to affirm a pharaoh's stability and continued rule?

At what Upper Egyptian city, believed to hold Osiris's actual burial site, did pilgrims gather annually for one of history's earliest recorded dramatic reenactments — a passion play depicting his death and resurrection?

How many pieces did Set cut Osiris's body into, according to one widely cited version of the myth — a number some scholars link to Egypt's traditional provincial divisions, each of which claimed to hold a piece?

What stretching-and-tearing effect from a black hole's tidal forces is actually gentler at the event horizon of a giant supermassive black hole than at a small stellar-mass one — meaning an astronaut could, in theory, cross a supermassive black hole's horizon without being ripped apart on the spot?

What theoretical form of radiation causes black holes to slowly lose mass and eventually evaporate over almost inconceivably long timescales — implying that, despite their name, they aren't perfectly black after all?

What long-standing puzzle in theoretical physics asks whether the details of whatever falls into a black hole are truly wiped out once the hole evaporates away — a direct clash between quantum mechanics and general relativity?

What hypothetical wall of extreme-energy radiation, proposed by physicists in 2012, would instantly incinerate anything crossing a black hole's event horizon — directly contradicting Einstein's prediction that a falling observer should feel nothing unusual there?

What process lets some black holes end up far more massive than any single collapsing star could ever produce — layer upon layer, as smaller black holes combine with each other again and again across cosmic history, revealed by growing catalogs of gravitational-wave detections?
What microscopic eight-legged invertebrate, nicknamed the water bear, survives being frozen, boiled, dried out, and irradiated by shutting down into a barely-alive state called a tun?

What German pastor and naturalist published the first scientific description of tardigrades in 1773, after spotting the creatures wriggling through a rain-gutter sediment sample under his microscope, and nicknamed them 'little water bears'?
What does 'Tardigrada' — the scientific name Italian biologist Lazzaro Spallanzani gave tardigrades in 1776 — literally translate to, referring to their plodding gait?
What tardigrade-specific protein, when spliced into human cell cultures, roughly halved the DNA damage those cells suffered from X-ray radiation by physically shielding their genome?

What Israeli spacecraft crash-landed on the Moon in April 2019 while carrying thousands of dehydrated tardigrades sealed inside a nickel 'lunar library' disc, raising an unresolved question about whether any of them survived the impact?
What Hokkien Chinese word for a fermented fish sauce, introduced to southern China by Vietnamese fishermen roughly 500 years ago, gave English the word 'ketchup'?
Before tomatoes took over as the standard base, what fungus was the most popular ingredient for the ketchup recipes filling 18th-century British cookbooks?
What Philadelphia scientist published the first known tomato-based ketchup recipe in 1812, a full century after fish- and mushroom-based ketchups had already spread through Europe?
What number, combining his own lucky digit with his wife's, did H.J. Heinz pick out of thin air for his famous ketchup-bottle slogan in 1896, despite his company already making more than 60 products?
What branch of physics, named from the Greek word for 'flow,' explains why ketchup sits stubbornly in the bottle until a sharp enough tap suddenly makes it gush?
What term describes ground -- soil, rock, or sediment -- that has stayed at or below the freezing point of water for at least two consecutive years, no matter how much snow or ice sits on top of it?

What name do scientists give to the ice-rich, Ice Age-era type of permafrost found across Siberia and Alaska that packs in roughly a quarter of all the organic carbon locked in frozen ground worldwide, despite covering only a small share of the permafrost region?

What genus of giant, amoeba-infecting virus did French scientists revive alive from a 48,500-year-old chunk of Siberian permafrost in 2023, the discovery behind headlines about 'zombie viruses' thawing out of the Arctic?
A 2018 USGS study found frozen Arctic permafrost holds about twice as much of what toxic, silvery heavy metal as all the world's oceans, atmosphere, and other soils combined?

What nickname do observers give to boreal forests, common across permafrost regions of Alaska and Siberia, where the trees end up leaning every which way once the frozen ground under their roots thaws unevenly and subsides?

What is the name for the outbreak that began in Strasbourg in July 1518, when a woman known as Frau Troffea started dancing alone in the street and couldn't stop, and by the following month roughly 400 townspeople had joined her in uncontrollable dancing?

Believing that Strasbourg's stricken dancers of 1518 needed to sweat their affliction out rather than be restrained, what type of buildings did the city's authorities clear out and turn into dance floors, complete with hired musicians and a wooden stage?

Which saint, blamed in German folklore for cursing people with uncontrollable dancing, did Strasbourg officials eventually send the worst-afflicted 1518 dancers on a three-day wagon journey to a shrine of, complete with red shoes and holy water?

What toxic mold that grows on damp rye, capable of causing spasms and hallucinations, has been proposed as an explanation for the 1518 Strasbourg dancing mania but is now largely dismissed by historians?

What term do historians such as John Waller use for the stress-triggered group behavior they believe explains the 1518 Strasbourg dancing mania, pointing to the famine and disease bearing down on the city's residents that year?
What antibacterial enzyme did Alexander Fleming discover seven years before penicillin, after a drop of his own nasal mucus happened to dissolve bacteria on a petri dish?
What fruit, found moldy on a Peoria, Illinois grocery shelf in 1943, yielded the highly productive Penicillium strain that became the ancestor of nearly all industrial penicillin made since?
During WWII penicillin shortages, hospitals recovered and reused the drug from what bodily fluid, since most of an injected dose passes through the kidneys chemically unchanged?

Pfizer's WWII breakthrough in mass-producing penicillin relied on deep-tank fermentation technology the company had first developed years earlier to manufacture what common food and drink additive from mold?
Widespread penicillin use in WWII helped cut the death rate from bacterial pneumonia among American soldiers from about 18% in the previous world war to under what percentage?
What small Buddhist kingdom in the eastern Himalayas, wedged between India and China, measures its national progress with a 'Gross National Happiness' index instead of GDP?
What 7,570-meter peak in Bhutan, whose name translates to 'White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers,' holds the title of the world's tallest mountain never to have been climbed?
What Bhutanese king coined the term 'Gross National Happiness' in 1972, declaring it more important than Gross Domestic Product as a measure of his country's progress?
Bhutan's constitution permanently requires the country to maintain forest cover of at least what percentage of its total land area?
In what year did Bhutan become the last country in the world to legalize television and the internet?

What English fossil collector, born in 1799 to a poor cabinet-maker's family in the seaside town of Lyme Regis, spent her life digging prehistoric marine reptiles out of the crumbling cliffs of England's Jurassic Coast to sell to collectors and scientists?
At just 12 years old, Mary Anning spent months excavating the first correctly identified skeleton of what extinct marine reptile from a Lyme Regis cliff in 1811-1812?

A 1800 lightning strike killed the nurse and two other children sheltering with 15-month-old Mary Anning under a tree — what was the name of the nurse who died, an event locals later credited with sparking the infant's unusual liveliness?

Inspired directly by Mary Anning's fossil finds, what 1830 painting by her friend Henry De la Beche became the first-ever pictorial reconstruction of prehistoric life based on fossil evidence, its print sales used to support Anning financially?

What term did geologist William Buckland coin for the fossilized feces Mary Anning helped identify inside ichthyosaur skeletons, which the pair used to reconstruct the diets of prehistoric marine reptiles?
What term describes the fiber-optic lines laid along ocean floors that physically carry the overwhelming majority of the world's intercontinental internet and phone traffic, rather than satellites?
What predator bit through an unarmored AT&T deep-sea fiber-optic cable at least four times in the mid-1980s, forcing engineers to start wrapping future undersea lines in protective armor?

About what percentage of yearly undersea cable faults are caused by fishing gear and dragged ship anchors combined, according to industry damage records, dwarfing the share caused by sharks or sabotage?
What repurposed steamship, the largest vessel afloat at the time, finally laid a durable transatlantic telegraph cable in 1866 after an 1858 attempt failed within weeks?
What natural conductor do many submarine cable systems use to complete the electrical circuit that powers signal-boosting repeaters along their length, instead of running a second wire back to shore?
What conductor led the orchestra through Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring at its chaotic 1913 Paris premiere, continuing to play despite objects being hurled at the musicians?

What 1940 Walt Disney animated feature paid Stravinsky $6,000 to reuse The Rite of Spring's score for a segment on the origins of life and the age of dinosaurs, a reworking he only decades later condemned as an 'imbecility'?
What music-theory term describes the technique -- layering an E-flat-seventh chord over an F-flat major chord -- behind the famous stabbing chord that opens The Rite of Spring's 'Augurs of Spring'?
What Ballets Russes impresario, who had already scored hits with Stravinsky's Firebird and Petrushka, commissioned The Rite of Spring as a third collaboration in 1911?
What word, used ever since to describe the pandemonium at The Rite of Spring's 1913 premiere, is absent from every contemporary newspaper account and didn't attach to the event until a 1924 revival?

What major Mesoamerican deity, honored as a wind god, patron of priests, and embodiment of the planet Venus, was worshipped continuously from Teotihuacan's earliest temples through the height of the Aztec Empire?

What Spanish historian, who never set foot in the Americas, first published in 1552 -- three decades after the conquest -- the now largely discredited claim that the Aztecs mistook Hernan Cortes for a returning god?
What unusual shape did Aztec temples dedicated to Ehecatl, Quetzalcoatl's wind-god aspect, typically take, so that gusts could pass around the building without a flat wall to catch them?

In Toltec legend, the exiled priest-king Topiltzin-Quetzalcoatl vowed to return in a specific calendar year that, by an eerie coincidence later exploited by Spanish chroniclers, also matched the year Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico. What was that calendar year called?

In one Aztec creation myth, Quetzalcoatl traveled to the underworld Mictlan and gathered the bones of a previous, destroyed humanity, then used what substance of his own to bring a new human race to life?

What term did NASA scientists coin for the charged icy particles that spiral down from Saturn's rings into its atmosphere along magnetic field lines, a process expected to fully deplete the rings within roughly 100 to 300 million years?
Despite stretching roughly 280,000 kilometers across, Saturn's main rings are, on average, only about how many meters thick?

What mysterious dark, wedge-shaped features drifting across Saturn's rings -- seen by Voyager in the early 1980s, then absent from view for years before reappearing -- are thought to be dust grains temporarily lifted by static electricity?

What name did NASA give the final 22 dive orbits that threaded the Cassini spacecraft between Saturn and its rings, letting scientists measure the rings' mass and estimate their age at just 10 to 100 million years -- far younger than Saturn itself?
What term describes small moons like Prometheus and Pandora, which use their gravity to confine Saturn's narrow F ring into a sharp, tight band rather than letting it spread out?

What group of roughly 500 brilliantly colored marine crustacean species, not true shrimp at all but a separate lineage called stomatopods that split off over 400 million years ago, is famous for having some of the fastest and most powerful strikes in the animal kingdom?
When a mantis shrimp's club-like claw strikes prey, the collapsing cavitation bubble it leaves behind briefly flashes to a temperature comparable to the surface of what astronomical object?
How many distinct types of color-sensing photoreceptors do mantis shrimp eyes contain -- four times what humans have, yet oddly not put to use for finer color discrimination?

What term, borrowed from a French crystallographer who first described the pattern in mollusk shells, names the twisted, helicoidal stacking of mineral fiber layers inside a mantis shrimp's claw that helps filter out damaging shear waves from its own strikes?
What common name is given to a spearing species of mantis shrimp whose mated pairs can stay bonded to the same partner and share a single burrow for up to 20 years?

What Japanese chemist, savoring the deep flavor of his wife's kelp broth in 1908, isolated glutamic acid from the kelp and coined a Japanese word for the taste it produced, later commercializing it as monosodium glutamate?

What Maryland pediatrician's speculative 1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine, describing numbness and palpitations after eating at Chinese restaurants, is now credited with launching decades of unfounded fear around a common seasoning?
What three-letter U.S. FDA safety designation, shared with staples like sugar and salt, has monosodium glutamate carried since the food-additive regulatory framework was created in 1958?
Among common foods, which long-aged Italian cheese can pack over 2,000 milligrams of naturally occurring free glutamate per 100 grams -- more than almost any other food, MSG-seasoned or not?

In what year did researchers identify a dedicated taste-bud receptor that responds specifically to glutamate, giving physiological proof that umami is a genuine fifth basic taste alongside sweet, sour, salty, and bitter?
What reddish mineral, worn from Antarctica's bedrock and frozen into the base of ice shelves, gives some Antarctic icebergs their eerie emerald-green color instead of the usual blue-white?
In what year was the International Ice Patrol established to track North Atlantic icebergs, less than a year after the Titanic disaster?
The largest iceberg ever reliably recorded, B-15, calved from Antarctica's Ross Ice Shelf in 2000 with a surface area comparable in size to which Caribbean island nation?
What East German leader publicly declared in June 1961, 'No one has any intention of building a wall,' just two months before secretly overseeing the overnight construction of the Berlin Wall?
What was the raked-gravel no-man's-land between the Berlin Wall's two parallel barriers called, cleared and floodlit so guards could spot the footprints of anyone attempting to cross?

Which flustered East German Politburo spokesman's mistaken answer of 'immediately, without delay' at a November 9, 1989 press conference sent crowds surging to the checkpoints and accidentally triggered the Berlin Wall's sudden fall that same night?

Frederick Banting, Charles Best, and James Collip patented their insulin extraction process in 1923, then sold that patent to the University of Toronto for what token sum, declaring the discovery belonged to the world?

What 14-year-old Toronto boy became the first person ever treated with insulin, in January 1922, surviving an impurity-triggered allergic reaction to the first injection before a more purified second dose brought his blood sugar down within a day?
When the 1923 Nobel Prize for insulin went only to Frederick Banting and John Macleod, excluding two key collaborators, Banting protested by splitting his prize money with which graduate student?
What is the official height, in meters, of Mount Everest, according to the 2020 joint measurement announced by Nepal and China?
What Nepali Sherpa mountaineer, climbing alongside New Zealander Edmund Hillary, became one of the first two people confirmed to reach the summit of Mount Everest, in 1953?
